newsitem.title: UK: EU grain prices buoyed by export, Brussels news.
newsitem.headline: EU grain prices buoyed by export, Brussels news.

text.p: European Union grain prices were generally firmer this week, buoyed by demand news and growing expectations that the EU would resume subsidised wheat sales.
The EU, at its weekly grain auction on Thursday, brought back subsidies that were suspended since last year when prices were at record highs.
It earlier also formally scrapped its nine-month-old export tax system, signalling subsidy bidding to go ahead to help cope with larger-than-expected new crop wheat.
French wheat was firmer, mostly helped by fresh export prospects, dealers said.
French wheat into Rouen was quoted at 890 francs on September delivery and at 885 francs on October/december delivery, up five on Tuesday but unchanged from Monday.

French wheat was underpinned by news Egypt bought 450,000 tonnes of French wheat on Sunday and by hopes the EU would finally ease its restritive grip on exports and grant wheat export refunds (subsidies) at its weekly grain tenders.
Traders in France had bid to export 379,250 tonnes of EU soft wheat at refunds ranging from 0.74 to 13.97 Ecus per tonne.
The EU ended up granting 237,470 tonnes of soft wheat at a maximum refund of 4.97 Ecus per tonne.
Rouen barley gained five francs to 865 francs on Sept/Dec delivery, helped by news Saudi Arabia was seeking 1.72 million tonnes of barley for October-December shipment.
Maize into Bordeaux was broadly unchanged at 890 francs per tonne on Oct-Dec delivery. Dealers said scattered rain was disrupting the first cuttings of maize in France's southwest.
In Germany, export prices of barley and rye were raised this week amid buying interest and hopes of intervention sales.
Prices of average wheat qualities held steady as European and domestic buyers were active but top qualities were marked down on lack of trade.
German farmers were in the last stages of the grain harvest and busy storing and drying grain. Brokers said many planned on retaining quality wheat to achieve better prices in 1997.
Polish buyers were in the market for bread wheat and feed wheat from Germany and Denmark but buying slowed whenever logistics facilities were too busy to handle more grain.
British feed wheat was sold at competitive prices around 270 marks a tonne cif for 1996 dates.
The Hamburg grain exchange this week kept its new crop bread wheat price (12.5 percent, 220 hagberg) steady at 287.50 marks and feed wheat was also unchanged at 275 marks.
The fob bread wheat offer range was steady at around 290 marks for low protein while 13-14 percent protein was slightly lower in a 295-317.50 marks range.
Spot export barley rose five marks at the top to 250-265 marks fob, bread rye remained at just under 260 marks fob and feed rye was up 12 marks at around 257 marks fob."

Wheat prices in the UK seesawed on crop and export news. Prices rose early in the week on news of the EU export tax news but retreated later after some UK forecasters revised upwards their 1996/97 crop estimates.

In Spain, maize sellers marked up their prices as rain delayed harvesting in the southwestern region of Extremadura. But dealers in Madrid expect prices to start sliding when the harvests reach the market and because of pressure from French maize imports.
Milling wheat has been of poor quality this year, and supply is limited, they said.
